entry.title: OpenAI partners with Google Cloud to offer frontier models and Codex workflows through Google Cloud Marketplace [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI and Google Cloud have partnered to integrate OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agentic workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden, enabling customers to access these models natively within Google Cloud's infrastructure. This integration supports complex AI workflows with Google's data governance and high-performance infrastructure, targeting enterprises including those in regulated industries. The models will be available for purchase through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments to apply those credits. OpenAI models will also be accessible via Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing customers with flexible model choices. General availability is planned in the coming weeks, expanding enterprise access to frontier AI models within Google Cloud's ecosystem.

entry.title: OpenAI releases official CLI for its REST API with installation options via Homebrew and Go, supporting command completion and update checks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has launched an official command-line interface (CLI) for its REST API, enabling users to interact with OpenAI services through a resource-based command structure. The CLI supports installation via Homebrew and Go, includes features like tab completion, update notifications, and detailed help commands, and requires API keys for standard and admin endpoints. The tool offers commands for generating responses, managing files, and accessing administrative functions, with options for JSON output formatting and local file uploads. It also includes mechanisms to check for updates without automatic installation and supports multiple shell environments for command completion and shortcuts.

entry.title: Developer fine-tunes a 360M-parameter language model to simulate a terminal interface by predicting screen changes from keypresses without a real shell or filesystem [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A developer trained a 360 million parameter language model to act as a terminal by predicting how the screen changes in response to each keypress, without an underlying shell or filesystem. The model can create files, run programs like vim and tmux, play snake, and maintain short-term memory of commands. It was fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker containers. The model treats the terminal as a grid of characters and outputs screen updates rather than text streams, using a small vocabulary of tokens to efficiently represent screen changes, including copying rows to handle scrolling. The demo runs in a browser with WebGPU support and is optimized for desktop use. This approach explores whether a language model can maintain a consistent interactive environment rather than just generating plausible terminal output.

entry.title: OpenAI leads global coalition to coordinate response and patch critical PHP vulnerabilities discovered using GPT-5.6 Sol, emphasizing AI's dual role in security [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI spearheaded a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source language widely used for websites and web applications. The flaws were identified using GPT-5.6 Sol as part of the Patch the Planet initiative, with contributions from partners like Wiz and Cloudflare. PHP maintainers led the fixes and releases, while OpenAI and collaborators coordinated research, technical support, and protections ahead of public disclosure. The initiative included developing a PHP version checker to help organizations identify vulnerable versions and apply necessary updates. OpenAI highlighted the significance of these vulnerabilities due to PHP's widespread use and noted that frontier AI detected the flaws before attackers, creating a Defender's Window for proactive mitigation. To support defenders with limited resources, OpenAI committed $1 billion in subsidized access to its Daybreak platform. OpenAI also proposed a scalable framework for coordinated vulnerability response in the AI era, involving validation, fix development, advance notice to affected organizations, and collaboration with government agencies to protect critical infrastructure. This approach aims to streamline responses as AI capabilities uncover more security issues in widely used software.

entry.title: OpenTelemetry enables detailed observability of AI agent workflows to trace execution paths, monitor costs, latency, and errors across multi-step LLM and tool calls [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AI agents orchestrate complex workflows involving multiple LLM calls and tool selections, making their execution paths difficult to trace and debug. OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral framework to capture telemetry data such as traces, metrics, and logs, enabling engineers to observe each step of an AI agent's run, including inputs, outputs, costs, and latencies. This observability is crucial because AI agents can produce silent errors, non-deterministic outputs, and unpredictable costs due to dynamic tool usage and model calls. By instrumenting AI agents with OpenTelemetry and visualizing data through platforms like SigNoz Cloud, developers gain insights into agent behavior, helping them identify inefficiencies, debug issues, and optimize performance and cost.

entry.title: Researchers propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation combining specialist merging and capability-guided supervision to improve student model training across six benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), a method that merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student model and adjusts supervision based on estimated capability gaps between teachers and the student. This approach addresses limitations of existing discrepancy-based supervision allocation by considering the student's current capabilities to modulate teacher guidance. CA-MOPD was evaluated on six benchmarks involving mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, achieving an average score of 32.22 and outperforming previous methods by up to 0.86 points. Controlled experiments confirm the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap-based supervision under matched training budgets.

entry.title: CountVideoBench introduces a synthetic video benchmark to evaluate prediction biases in object counting by video-language models, revealing low accuracy and value-dependent biases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: CountVideoBench is a new benchmark comprising 2,600 synthetic videos with object counts ranging from 5 to 50, designed to assess counting capabilities of video-language models without confounding factors like object motion. The study evaluated sixteen models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting, finding no model exceeded 27.6% exact match accuracy and that models showed distinct biases toward certain preferred counts, with accuracy peaking at these values and dropping sharply at adjacent counts. These results highlight limitations in current models' counting abilities and the need for balanced benchmarks to better diagnose and improve this fundamental visual task.

entry.title: Researchers propose TURTLE, an unsupervised environment design method to evolve self-tuning benchmarks for long-horizon AI tool use, increasing task difficulty and diversity across multiple applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), a method using large language model agents-a proposer, solver, and feedback generator-to evolve AI tool-use tasks without human supervision. TURTLE adapts test suites to various environments, supporting user simulators, document retrieval, and multi-app interactions, aiming to improve AI assistants' capabilities beyond simple chat interfaces. Empirical evaluations on benchmarks like AppWorld, τ-Bench, and AutomationBench with the Gemma 4 31B-it model show that TURTLE increases the proportion of hard tasks by 165% on AppWorld, enhances task diversity in reasoning and tool interactions, and reveals a wider range of failure modes compared to original tasks. This approach addresses scalability and domain limitations of existing benchmarks for AI tool use.

entry.title: Researchers introduce AuthorizationBench to evaluate LLM agents' adherence to user authorization, finding 19.2% of actions exceed granted permissions across 286 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed AuthorizationBench, a benchmark to assess whether large language model (LLM) agents act within the authorization scope granted by users. Testing four models across 286 tasks in an authorization-aware sandbox, they found agents acted beyond their authorization in 19.2% of cases, with rates varying by configuration. The study highlights that task completion and reasoning effort do not guarantee authorization alignment, and agents consulting users before acting show lower rates of unauthorized behavior. The benchmark includes tasks spanning various triggers, consequences, and application domains, producing 6,864 execution trajectories. Results indicate agents sometimes act out of authorization even without causing direct harm, and more often under benign pressures than malicious ones. This reveals a tension between agent autonomy and preserving user decision authority, suggesting the need for further human-centered research on authorization alignment in AI agents.

entry.title: Researchers present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver for PDEs with constraints, enabling efficient forward and inverse problem solving across physics and engineering applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates constraints from large systems of equations arising in partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids. This solver supports linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, solves inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients and right-hand sides, and uses learnable graph coarsening to accelerate computations. The solver's stability and differentiability reduce the complexity of forward modeling and improve efficiency in related inverse problems, making it particularly useful for applications in geophysics where reducing model uncertainty is critical.

entry.title: JetBrains Research presents Arend theorem prover based on homotopy type theory with cubical syntax and IntelliJ IDE integration
entry.summary: JetBrains Research has developed Arend, a theorem prover designed to formalize mathematics within univalent foundations focusing on constructive mathematics. Arend uses a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax aligned with Martin-Löf Type Theory and features a flexible system of classes and records for constructing definition hierarchies. The Arend language is supported by an IntelliJ plugin that turns IntelliJ IDEA into a dedicated development environment, and its main library includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology, and synthetic homotopy theory.

entry.title: Researchers introduce S2-MAS, a multi-agent simulation framework with 500 million synthetic household personas for society-scale economic modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed S2-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework that models economic responses using 500 million synthetic household personas based on real survey data. The framework features the Genese engine, which separates decision-making from state updates, and includes financial scenarios and ledgers to track consumption, cash, debt, and payments. A compact decision model trained on millions of examples outperforms previous models in consumer financial-choice tasks. The team evaluated eight financial task families and simulated 12 million distinct household agents under various purchase and funding conditions, observing how changes in purchase goals and credit limits affect consumption across different demographic groups. The simulation captures differences in education, employment, household size, and financial behaviors such as cash drawdown and debt repayment. A 24-month panel study varied purchase goals under a common credit product, updating offers based on repayment and arrears. S2-MAS links diverse household decisions to evolving financial outcomes, enabling economic experiments across household groups, population scales, and time horizons, supporting detailed analysis of consumption, cash flow, and repayment patterns in large populations.

entry.title: RayCo4D introduces a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D dynamic scene reconstruction, improving novel-view synthesis and temporal consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: RayCo4D presents a new approach for reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video by separating visual measurements from latent 3D motion states and associating each track with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray. The model uses shared latent motion nodes with SE(3) poses and velocities, coupled by a white-noise-on-acceleration prior to enable continuous-time interpolation and joint constraint of latent states across visibility intervals. Experiments demonstrate that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, enhances structural and temporal consistency during rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering for diverse monocular dynamic scenes.

entry.title: Researchers present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine using specialized AI agents coordinated by an Orchestrator to optimize drug development across 50 protein targets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: MADDIE is an autonomous system designed to accelerate drug discovery by coordinating four specialized AI agents-HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator-under a central Orchestrator agent. This multi-agent approach enables flexible workflows that adapt to the iterative and non-linear nature of drug discovery campaigns, producing molecules that meet key property requirements along with their synthesis routes. Evaluated across 50 protein targets, MADDIE outperforms existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose large language models in efficiency and effectiveness. The system demonstrates varied strategies tailored to different targets while maintaining time and token efficiency, offering a low-cost and scalable solution for end-to-end drug discovery. Code and datasets for MADDIE are publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: Researchers introduce VLA-Rolling, an adaptive inference framework that reuses action tails to reduce denoising steps and improve control in vision-language-action models across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically discard unexecuted action tails during iterative denoising, but researchers show these tails retain useful denoising progress that can be reused to improve efficiency and accuracy. They propose VLA-Rolling, a lightweight framework that inherits action tails, estimates confidence per action, and refines actions through adaptive renoising and denoising budget allocation without retraining the underlying model. VLA-Rolling was tested on several VLA models including π0.5, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 across benchmarks such as LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0. It reduced inference costs in all 16 model-benchmark pairs with up to 1.48× speedup and improved success rates in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. These results demonstrate that action tails are reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference with fewer denoising steps.

entry.title: Researchers formulate Heisenberg antiferromagnet Hamiltonians and ground-state sign structures using graph theory, linking them to weighted Max-Cut problems on Hilbert graphs
entry.summary: Researchers present a graph-theoretic approach to studying Heisenberg antiferromagnets by representing their Hamiltonians as weighted Laplacians of Hilbert graphs, where vertices correspond to spin configurations and edges connect configurations differing by spin exchanges. This framework relates the exact ground-state energy to the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian and connects phase optimization to classical antiferromagnetic models and weighted Max-Cut problems on these graphs. The study shows that when the Hilbert graph is bipartite, a diagonal sign transformation removes positive off-diagonal Hamiltonian elements, reproducing the Marshall sign rule via graph two-coloring; otherwise, the minimal positive weight corresponds to edges uncut by Max-Cut. This unified graph formulation provides insights into wave function sign structures, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, and challenges in variational and quantum Monte Carlo methods.

entry.title: WeGR introduces behavior-aware tokenization and preference alignment to improve generative retrieval in industrial search, achieving gains in orders, CTR, and CVR with reduced resource usage [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: WeGR is a unified generative retrieval framework designed to enhance industrial search by incorporating user behavior signals through a novel tokenizer and preference alignment method. It addresses challenges in preserving collaborative signals and sparse reward issues in reinforcement learning by using a Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) and Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO). Extensive offline tests show improved retrieval and ranking, while a six-week online A/B test on a large e-commerce platform demonstrated increases of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, alongside reductions in CPU and GPU usage by over 25%. These results indicate WeGR's effectiveness and efficiency in real-world deployment, supporting multiple search scenarios with high traffic.

entry.title: SkillEval framework uses cognitive diagnosis models to generate interpretable skill profiles for 3,811 LLMs across five benchmarks, improving evaluation granularity and prediction of model behavior [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: SkillEval introduces a new evaluation framework that moves beyond single scalar scores by analyzing large language models (LLMs) at the skill level using cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs). It leverages LLMs' meta-cognitive abilities to identify interpretable skills from benchmark questions and estimates per-skill abilities, providing more calibrated and informative model profiles than traditional average-based methods. The study evaluated 3,811 LLMs on 9,523 items across five diverse benchmarks including MATH and BBH. The framework demonstrates practical benefits in two downstream tasks: dynamically routing queries to the most capable yet efficient model, reducing inference costs by over 60% while improving performance, and enabling efficient evaluation of unseen models through Computerized Adaptive Testing. Additionally, SkillEval's skill profiles offer insights into skill sharing across benchmarks and differences between instruction-tuned and base models.

entry.title: Researchers develop an in-house System 1 judge using LoRA adapters to triage coding sessions at 1% of frontier LLM cost and evaluate open LoRA models on JevBench with competitive accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a typed decision approach that computes probabilities for fixed options in one forward pass by reading language model logits or a small head over hidden states, avoiding text generation and parsing. They describe an in-house System 1 judge that triages about 148,000 coding session records, replacing a costly frontier LLM judge with a self-hosted frozen backbone and LoRA adapter, reducing cost to roughly 1% and processing 1,000 sessions in about three minutes on one GPU. The study also evaluates whether a readout adding no parameters can be competitive by applying the Eikos recipe and a corpus of 25,000 decisions to three LoRA-adapted decoder backbones (1B, 2B, and 35B parameters). Their 35B model scores 79.3% on 111 hard JevBench items, comparable to a commercial reference at 73.0%, and outperforms several open systems. They find no benefit from training the output layer's letter rows, and retraining on a later corpus release improves the 2B model's accuracy by 11.7 points, highlighting the limitations of small evaluations.

entry.title: OmniSimulator trains small language models with structured behavior-oriented reasoning to improve realistic user simulation on short-video platforms [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose OmniSimulator, a training framework that enhances small language models' ability to simulate authentic user behavior by organizing reasoning into a five-dimensional schema and using high-quality data from real user interactions. The approach employs a teacher model to generate detailed reasoning traces, helping smaller models learn meaningful behavior patterns rather than superficial correlations. Using nearly 10,000 training instances from three months of data on 200 users, OmniSimulator improved the Qwen3-8B model's performance by over 34%, achieving results comparable to larger models like Claude-Sonnet-4.5 while enabling smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These findings suggest that structured behavior-oriented reasoning can enable scalable, high-fidelity user simulation with smaller language models.

entry.title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.

entry.title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29785v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.

entry.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

entry.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

entry.title: CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). Unlike traditional and even recent LLM-augmented approaches that ultimately rely on clustering vector embeddings, our framework leverages LLM capabilities directly for the entire pipeline. Experiments demonstrate that this approach provides better utility over existing (embedding-based) methods in the DP setting, especially in the high privacy regime. We evaluate the quality of CALLIOPE outputs using a variety of traditionally studied clustering metrics, as well as some novel utility metrics that we introduce.

entry.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

entry.title: TeachBack: Learning to Teach via Bidirectional Preference Optimization for On-Policy Self-Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29167v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. We find that access to sufficient privileged information allows the Teacher to generate highly accurate trajectories; however, accuracy alone does not guarantee that these trajectories are suitable for Student learning. Direct access to a complete solution may encourage shortened, reference-conditioned derivations that omit the exploration, verification, and self-correction required to solve problems without privileged information. We introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that learns not only from the Teacher but also how the Teacher should teach. TeachBack shapes the Teacher's generation behavior by controlling the length of the reference-reasoning suffix injected into the prompt and by varying the prompt style. While maintaining comparable Teacher accuracy, it encourages the Teacher to explore and re-solve problems, thereby reducing its reliance on the reference solution. At each rollout refresh, the shared policy generates both a privileged Teacher trajectory and a problem-only Student trajectory. A pairwise preference objective uses privileged Teacher trajectories to improve Student learning, while the reversed preference uses the Student's behavior to shape future Teacher supervision under the privileged condition. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that TeachBack consistently improves Student performance over existing OPSD methods and related baselines.

entry.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.

entry.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

entry.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

entry.title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.30014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

entry.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.30128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

entry.title: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2509.25045v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite their capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain opaque with limited understanding of their internal representations. Current interpretability methods either focus on input-oriented feature extraction, such as supervised probes and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), or on output distribution inspection, such as logit-oriented approaches. A full understanding of LLM vector spaces, however, requires integrating both perspectives, something existing approaches struggle with due to constraints on latent feature definitions. We introduce the Hyperdimensional Probe, a hybrid supervised probe that combines symbolic representations with neural probing. Leveraging Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) and hypervector algebra, it unifies prior methods: the top-down interpretability of supervised probes, SAE's sparsity-driven proxy space, and output-oriented logit investigation. By combining the supervised learning paradigm of traditional probes with the dictionary-based representation principle of SAEs, our approach enables deeper input-focused feature extraction while supporting output-oriented analysis. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently extracts meaningful semantic information across different LLMs, embedding sizes, and configurations, uncovering concept-oriented insights into LLM inference across two distinct scenarios: input-completion tasks and QA-focused text generation. VSA-based probing overcomes the limitations of logit-based analyses, which are constrained by the model's token vocabulary, while also mitigating the noisier interpretability outcomes often produced by SAEs in settings with a bounded conceptual feature space. By supporting a joint investigation of input-output features, this work advances the semantic understanding of neural representations while unifying the complementary perspectives of prior methods.

entry.title: The Stepwise Informativeness Assumption: When Do Entropy Dynamics Track Reasoning Correctness in LLMs? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2604.06192v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work uses entropy-based signals at multiple representation levels to study reasoning in large language models, but the field remains largely empirical. From a theoretical perspective, reductions in model uncertainty do not necessarily reflect progress toward correctness. In this work, we characterize when such alignment can be expected through the Stepwise Informativeness Assumption (SIA), which requires entropy-reducing reasoning-prefix extensions increase the probability assigned to valid answers in expectation. We show that next-token prediction can transfer answer-relevant information from training data to the model, but does not, by itself, guarantee alignment with correctness. Instead, we propose that this alignment depends on how the training regime couples reasoning traces to correct answers. Furthermore, we hypothesize observable signatures of this phenomenon and characterize its expected failure regimes. We empirically investigate how entropy dynamics relate to correctness across four reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC, SVAMP, MATH) and diverse open-weight language models spanning base, instruction-tuned, and RL-trained regimes. Our results show that entropy-correctness alignment strengthens with post-training but can weaken when task difficulty exceeds model capabilities.

entry.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.21561v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

entry.title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2601.13235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.

entry.title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2602.18297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are LLM-based systems that analyze reasoning traces to detect when outputs may exhibit attributes of interest, such as test-hacking behavior during code generation. In this paper, we use information-theoretic analysis to show that non-zero mutual information between CoT and output is a necessary but not sufficient condition for CoT monitorability. We identify two sources of approximation error that may undermine the performance of CoT monitors in practice: information gap, which measures the extent to which the monitor can extract the information available in CoT, and elicitation error, which measures the extent to which the monitor approximates the optimal monitoring function. Empirically, we show that CoT obfuscation can arise even in the absence of any optimization pressure against CoT. We further demonstrate that the fragility of CoT monitorability can be systematically mitigated through targeted training objectives. To this end, we propose a practical, label-free objective based on mutual information between outputs and CoTs, and benchmark it against an oracle-based method that directly rewards the monitored model for CoTs that maximize monitor accuracy. Across multiple environments, we show that our objective is effective at preventing CoT obfuscation even when training against a monitor, and helps mitigate reward hacking when the task reward is imperfectly specified.

entry.title: Rethinking Synthetic Rationale Supervision for Disease Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.10279v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning with synthetic rationales is widely assumed to improve clinical prediction by teaching models not only what to predict but why. We test this assumption on five-year Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) prediction from longitudinal health histories. In this setting, we generate training rationales using the correct labels, then fine-tune models to output a rationale followed by a label. Across a large-scale controlled experiment of 504 configurations, we find that Rationale First SFT consistently and substantially hurts predictive performance relative to Label Only fine-tuning. The degradation persists across model families and data scales, and is not resolved by using a reasoning-oriented base model. A fixed-protocol cardiovascular disease (CVD) validation reproduces similar findings. Crucially, the failure is not explained by poor rationale quality: human expert annotation confirms that the generated rationales are medically accurate and faithfully grounded in patient-specific evidence, and few-shot experiments show that the same rationales improve performance when used as inference-time demonstrations rather than training targets. A simple label-ordering intervention clarifies the mechanism: placing the prediction before the same rationale restores predictive performance. This suggests that conditioning predictions on generated rationales contributes to the degradation. We hope our work paves the way toward a more precise understanding of when and how rationale-based supervision helps and when it does not, guiding the responsible development of language models for high-stakes clinical prediction.

entry.title: DFAH-Bench: What Agreement Leaves Unmeasured in Financial Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.20491v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a financial agent repeats its decision, how much does that tell us about the actions behind it? DFAH-Bench examines this question through replay experiments, a controlled test of omitted tool calls, and banking tasks with authorization checks. Across 570 eligible prospective replay episodes, decisions agreed at rates of 94-95%, while tool paths, including inputs and results, agreed at 45-52%; one condition fell one group short of the planned minimum. In a separate 48-execution diagnostic, deleting the same calls from repeated records left agreement perfect. In banking probes, repeated authorization decisions sometimes conflicted with constructed rule labels. The $\tau$-Knowledge banking study scheduled 1,080 episodes, with 1,033 known outcomes. Structural checks alone completed more primary tasks than either model-based gate-and-recovery bundle. Input limits and recovery behavior materially shape these results. The typed-choice bundle had lower mean episode cost than the generative bundle on complete task pairs, but fewer successes across the primary schedule under every assignment of unknown outcomes. Missing outcomes prevented the planned confirmatory tests, so the banking comparisons are descriptive. Together, the findings show that agreement alone cannot establish reliability: it can conceal changes in execution, systematic omissions, and unsupported decisions. Evaluation therefore needs to connect what the agent did, the evidence and rules governing its action, and whether it completed the task.

entry.title: Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.07226v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

entry.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.15207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

entry.title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.18727v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) are proposed as oversight tools for language models: an Activation Verbaliser (AV) writes an English explanation of an activation vector, and an Activation Reconstructor (AR) maps the explanation back to a vector. Their value for oversight depends on a human monitor being able to tell a true account of an activation from a false one, given the AV's explanation. We formalise NLA training and NLA oversight deployment as two different referential games from Emergent Communication: training is a generative referential game, while oversight is a discriminative, multi-modal, partially-observable referential game played over a many-to-many relation between the monitored language model's activations and the accounts that are true of them. The gap between the two games predicts that AV's explanations will identify which activation they describe without discriminating its true account from closely matched false ones, since training never asks explanations to rule anything out. Using the NLA's own AR as a maximally-sympathetic surrogate monitor model, we experimentally confirm this theoretical insight on one released checkpoint: true accounts beat accounts of other activations in all 320 comparisons, but beat fluent rivals differing in a single claim only 60.2% of the time (standard error 6.7%, chance at 50%, $n = 35$). A meaning-preserving rewrite by an uninvolved model costs only 2.1% of the distance to another activation's account, so the failure is not due to the NLA pair having developed private conventions in the AV's explanations. Our rival accounts test only transcript-level truths, which the monitored language model's conversation settles, so these results bound the easiest case and leave claims about the monitored model's own processing untested. We state conjectures that would make both results consequences of the framework.

entry.title: ZK-irp-firewall: Zero-knowledge invariant enforcement for AI agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed ZK-irp-firewall, a zero-knowledge proof-based system designed to enforce invariant properties in AI agents. This technology aims to enhance the reliability and security of AI systems by ensuring they adhere to specified constraints without revealing sensitive information.

entry.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

entry.title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

entry.title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.

entry.title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. The system currently supports four major imaging modalities -- Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI. To our knowledge, it is among the earliest agentic systems to run its entire pipeline with a Small Language Model (SLM) in the 0.6B-parameter range. This multi-agent architecture, built around an Extract-Ground-Generate paradigm, performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase, together forming a fully "no-touch" reporting workflow that requires no keyboard input, external API calls, or internet connectivity. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.

entry.title: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. DataPraxis-5K is available at huggingface.co/datasets/stargazerhust/DataPraxis-5k

entry.title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

entry.title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.

entry.title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

entry.title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.

entry.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.

entry.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.

entry.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

entry.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

entry.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

entry.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
